brief: Morgan Stanley's Andrew Sheets poses the puzzle: US 10-year yields are up 100bp this year while global equities are up about 13%, a tension the Gordon Growth model (dividends over r-g) explains only if growth expectations (g) have risen as fast as rates, which Sheets argues is happening amid buoyant markets. The piece is skeptical of that reading: excluding AI capex funded by new debt, US investment has been in recession for two years, and UBS data shows non-residential investment averaging 0.1% YoY (vs a 3.2% long-run average) and residential -2.0% YoY (vs 2.2%), while AI-related investment grew 26% YoY. Goldman's own decomposition finds the resilience puzzle smaller than it appears: Q3 GDP grew 3.4%, 2026 growth is forecast at 2.2% (only 0.3pp below the start-of-year estimate), financial conditions imply just a 0.1% GDP hit since higher equities, narrower credit spreads and a weaker dollar nearly offset higher rates, and the oil shock nets to a 0.3% hit after a capex offset. Consumption is the key beat: the forecast was cut from 2.4% to 2.0%, but incoming data tracks 2.2%. Flagged risk: a stock selloff would trigger a wealth-effect hit and likely tip the US into recession.
